module_title: Critical Phenomena, Crystal Defects & Solid Properties (Advanced)
introduction: Tailored for high-yield JEE Advanced analytics and deep conceptual NEET items. This level explores the liquefaction of gases (Critical Constants), macroscopic defects in crystal lattices, and the electrical and magnetic properties of solids derived from Band Theory.

core_concepts.title: Critical Phenomena (Andrews' Isotherms)
core_concepts.description:
A gas cannot be liquefied solely by applying pressure if its temperature is above its Critical Temperature ($T_c$). 
1. Critical Temperature: $T_c = \frac{8a}{27Rb}$. Above this, the kinetic energy overcomes attractive forces ($a$).
2. Critical Pressure: $P_c = \frac{a}{27b^2}$. Minimum pressure required to liquefy gas at $T_c$.
3. Critical Volume: $V_c = 3b$. Volume occupied by 1 mole of gas at $T_c$ and $P_c$.
At the critical point, the compressibility factor $Z_c = \frac{P_c V_c}{R T_c} = \frac{3}{8} = 0.375$ for all van der Waals gases.

core_concepts.title: Stoichiometric Defects in Solids
core_concepts.description:
Point defects that do not disturb the stoichiometry of the solid.
1. Schottky Defect: Equal number of cations and anions are completely missing from their lattice sites. This creates vacancies and significantly Lowers the Density of the crystal. Seen in highly ionic compounds with similar ion sizes (e.g., NaCl, KCl, CsCl).
2. Frenkel Defect: An ion (usually the smaller cation) leaves its normal site and occupies an interstitial site. It creates a vacancy defect at its original site and an interstitial defect at its new location. Density Remains Unchanged. Seen in compounds with large differences in ion sizes (e.g., AgCl, ZnS).

core_concepts.title: Non-Stoichiometric Defects & F-Centers
core_concepts.description:
Defects that alter the ratio of cations to anions.
1. Metal Excess Defect (Anionic Vacancies): An anion goes missing, and an electron occupies its vacancy to maintain electrical neutrality. This trapped electron is called an F-center (Farbenzenter). It is responsible for imparting color to the crystal (e.g., NaCl heated in Na vapor turns yellow).
2. Metal Deficiency Defect: Occurs in transition metals where a cation goes missing, and a nearby cation acquires a higher oxidation state to balance the charge (e.g., FeO, NiO).

core_concepts.title: Magnetic Properties of Solids
core_concepts.description:
1. Diamagnetic: Weakly repelled by a magnetic field. All electrons are paired (e.g., $TiO_2$, $NaCl$, $C_6H_6$).
2. Paramagnetic: Weakly attracted by a magnetic field due to the presence of unpaired electrons (e.g., $O_2$, $Cu^{2+}$, $Fe^{3+}$).
3. Ferromagnetic: Strongly attracted and can be permanently magnetized. Magnetic domains align strictly in the same direction (e.g., Fe, Co, Ni, $CrO_2$).
4. Antiferromagnetic: Domains align in exactly opposite directions, canceling out all magnetic moments. Net moment is zero (e.g., $MnO$).
5. Ferrimagnetic: Domains align in opposite directions but in unequal numbers. Net moment is small (e.g., $Fe_3O_4$, ferrites).

core_concepts.title: Bragg's Law (X-Ray Diffraction)
core_concepts.description: Used to determine the internal crystal structure and interplanar spacing ($d$) of a solid. When X-rays of wavelength $\lambda$ strike a crystal at an angle $\theta$, constructive interference (a diffraction peak) occurs if the path difference is an integral multiple of $\lambda$. Equation: $n\lambda = 2d \sin\theta$, where $n$ is the order of reflection (usually $n=1$).

important_entities.name: Boyle Temperature ($T_B$) vs Inversion Temperature ($T_i$)
important_entities.significance: Boyle Temperature ($T_B$) is the exact temperature at which a real gas behaves like an ideal gas over an appreciable pressure range (where $Z=1$). Inversion Temperature ($T_i$) is the temperature below which a gas undergoes cooling upon Joule-Thomson expansion (isenthalpic expansion). Note that $T_i = 2 T_B$.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A very frequent MCQ in both JEE and NEET: Silver Bromide ($AgBr$) is highly unique because it is the only common ionic solid that exhibits BOTH Schottky defects and Frenkel defects simultaneously in its crystal lattice.

According to simple Lewis dot structures, Oxygen ($O_2$) appears to have all electrons paired, suggesting it should be diamagnetic. However, experimentally, liquid oxygen is strongly attracted to a magnet. This is explained ONLY by Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT), which reveals two unpaired electrons in its anti-bonding $\pi^*$ orbitals, proving it is Paramagnetic.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Schottky is 'Shot' out; Frenkel is a 'Fake' position.
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Schottky sounds like 'Shot'—the ions are shot completely out of the crystal, so mass is lost and density decreases. Frenkel sounds like 'Fake'—the ion is still inside the crystal but in a fake (interstitial) position, so mass is retained and density remains the same.

exam_strategy_tips: In solid state stoichiometry problems (e.g., 'A forms CCP lattice, B occupies $2/3$ of tetrahedral voids'), always assume the number of atoms forming the main lattice is $N$ (or $4$ for FCC/CCP). Then TVs = $2N$, OVs = $N$. Calculate the number of B atoms ($2/3 \times 2N = 4N/3$). The formula is $A_N B_{4N/3}$, which simplifies by multiplying by 3 to get the empirical formula $A_3B_4$.
